summary.text: Factor the factorials at successive prime-power levels into powers of \(p\) and shifted blocks of residues coprime to \(p\); expanding each full block through degree two shows it is shift-independent modulo \(p^{3r}\), because the reciprocal sum vanishes modulo \(p^{2r}\), the reciprocal pair sum vanishes modulo \(p^r\), and all cubic terms contain \(p^{3r}\). The even case then follows by balancing block exponents, while the odd case uses the half-integer factorial formula and a prime-power Lehmer–Morley half-block identity—shifts are compensated by powers of \(4^{p^{r-1}(p-1)}\)—after which the matching unit factors can be cancelled.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\frac{\Gamma(9n+1)\Gamma(2n+1)\Gamma(3n/2+1)}
 {\Gamma(9n/2+1)\Gamma(4n+1)\Gamma(3n+1)\Gamma(n+1)}.
\]
Assume, as in the statement, that every \(a(n)\) is an integer. We prove that, for every prime \(p\geq 5\), every \(n\geq1\), and every \(r\geq1\),
\[
a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\]
Throughout the proof, when an integer represented by the real number \(a(m)\) is needed, we denote it by \(A_m\). Thus \(A_m\in\mathbb Z\) and its image in \(\mathbb R\) is \(a(m)\). The choice is in fact unique, but uniqueness is not needed.

We first establish the prime-power product congruences used in the factorial decompositions.

## 1. Reduced residues and harmonic sums

Fix a prime \(p\geq5\) and an integer \(r\geq1\), and put
\[
P=p^r,\qquad \varphi=p^{r-1}(p-1).
\]
Let
\[
\mathcal U=\{i:1\leq i<P,\ p\nmid i\}.
\]
This is a set of representatives for the units modulo \(P\).

We need three harmonic congruences. All inverses below are inverses in the indicated residue ring.

First,
\[
\sum_{i\in\mathcal U}i^{-1}\equiv0\pmod P,
\qquad
\sum_{i\in\mathcal U}i^{-2}\equiv0\pmod P. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, inversion permutes the units, so these sums equal respectively the sums of the first and second powers of all units modulo \(P\). Multiplication by \(2\) also permutes the units. If \(S_1\) is the sum of the units, then \(2S_1=S_1\), hence \(S_1=0\). If \(S_2\) is the sum of their squares, then \(4S_2=S_2\), so \(3S_2=0\). Since both \(2\) and \(3\) are units modulo \(P\), these assertions follow.

The elementary symmetric sum of degree two also vanishes modulo \(P\):
\[
E_2:=\sum_{\{i,j\}\subset\mathcal U,\ i\ne j}(ij)^{-1}\equiv0\pmod P. \tag{2}
\]
Here each unordered pair is counted once. This follows from
\[
\left(\sum_{i\in\mathcal U}i^{-1}\right)^2
 =\sum_{i\in\mathcal U}i^{-2}+2E_2
\]
and (1), because \(2\) is invertible modulo \(P\).

We also require the stronger congruence
\[
\sum_{i\in\mathcal U}i^{-1}\equiv0\pmod {P^2}. \tag{3}
\]
To prove it, pair \(i\) with \(P-i\). In \(\mathbb Z/P^2\mathbb Z\), the identity
\[
(P-i)^{-1}=-i^{-1}-P i^{-2}
\]
follows by multiplying the right side by \(P-i\); the error is a multiple of \(P^2\). Consequently
\[
i^{-1}+(P-i)^{-1}=-P i^{-2}\pmod {P^2}.
\]
Summing over all reduced residues and using that \(i\mapsto P-i\) permutes \(\mathcal U\), we obtain
\[
2\sum_{i\in\mathcal U}i^{-1}
 =-P\sum_{i\in\mathcal U}i^{-2}\pmod {P^2}.
\]
The sum of inverse squares is zero modulo \(P\) by (1), so the right side vanishes modulo \(P^2\). Since \(2\) is a unit, (3) follows.

These congruences imply a shifted full-block product identity. Work in
\[
R=\mathbb Z/P^3\mathbb Z=\mathbb Z/p^{3r}\mathbb Z.
\]
For every integer \(q\geq0\),
\[
\prod_{i\in\mathcal U}(qP+i)=\prod_{i\in\mathcal U}i\quad\text{in }R. \tag{4}
\]
To see this, factor each term as
\[
qP+i=i(1+qP/i).
\]
In \(R\), \((qP)^3=0\), so expansion of the product stops after degree two:
\[
\prod_{i\in\mathcal U}(1+qP/i)
 =1+qP\sum_i i^{-1}+(qP)^2\sum_{i<j}(ij)^{-1}.
\]
The linear term is zero because the first sum is divisible by \(P^2\), by (3), and the quadratic term is zero because the pair sum is divisible by \(P\), by (2). This proves (4).

Define the natural-number products
\[
W=W(p,r):=\prod_{i\in\mathcal U}i,
\]
\[
U(C,m)=U(C,m;p,r):=
 \prod_{q=0}^{Cm-1}\prod_{i\in\mathcal U}(qP+i).
\]
Equation (4) gives
\[
U(C,m)\equiv W^{Cm}\pmod {P^3}. \tag{5}
\]
Every factor involved is prime to \(p\), so \(W\), every \(U(C,m)\), and every shifted block introduced below are units modulo \(P^3\).

## 2. Half blocks and a prime-power Morley identity

Let
\[
\mathcal H=\left\{i:1\leq i\leq\frac{P-1}{2},\ p\nmid i\right\}.
\]
Since \(P\) is odd, negation \(i\mapsto P-i\) bijects \(\mathcal H\) with the upper half of \(\mathcal U\). The inverse squares of \(i\) and \(P-i\) agree modulo \(P\). Therefore the second congruence in (1) becomes
\[
2\sum_{i\in\mathcal H}i^{-2}\equiv0\pmod P,
\]
and hence
\[
\sum_{i\in\mathcal H}i^{-2}\equiv0\pmod P. \tag{6}
\]

In \(R=\mathbb Z/P^3\mathbb Z\), define the shifted half block
\[
B_q:=\prod_{i\in\mathcal H}(i+qP),\qquad q\geq0, \tag{7}
\]
and also
\[
B_-:=\prod_{i\in\mathcal H}(i-P).
\]
All these products are units in \(R\).

We next prove
\[
B_-=4^{\varphi}B_0. \tag{8}
\]
This is the prime-power Morley product calculation needed later.

Put, in \(R\),
\[
u_i=i^{-1},\qquad c=2^{-1},\qquad
H_1=\sum_{i\in\mathcal H}u_i,\qquad H_2=\sum_{i\in\mathcal H}u_i^2.
\]
Consider the Lehmer product
\[
L=\prod_{i\in\mathcal H}
 \frac{1-Pu_i}{1-Pcu_i}.
\]
Because \(P^3=0\) in \(R\),
\[
(1-Pcu_i)^{-1}=1+Pcu_i+P^2c^2u_i^2.
\]
Multiplication gives
\[
\frac{1-Pu_i}{1-Pcu_i}
 =1-Pcu_i-P^2c^2u_i^2.
\]
Expanding the product to degree two and using
\[
2\sum_{i<j}u_i u_j=H_1^2-H_2
\]
yields
\[
L=1-PcH_1+P^2c^3(H_1^2-3H_2). \tag{9}
\]

There is also an exact product evaluation of \(L\). For each \(i\in\mathcal H\),
\[
\frac{1-P/i}{1-P/(2i)}= rac{2(P-i)}{P-2i}. \tag{10}
\]
The reduced residues can be partitioned in two ways:
\[
\mathcal U=\mathcal H\sqcup(P-\mathcal H)

after splitting into lower and upper halves, and
\[
\mathcal U=2\mathcal H\sqcup(P-2\mathcal H)

after splitting into even and odd representatives. Both unions are disjoint. Comparing the products in these two decompositions and cancelling \(\prod_{i\in\mathcal H}i\) gives the exact integer identity
\[
\prod_{i\in\mathcal H}(P-i)
 =2^{|\mathcal H|}\prod_{i\in\mathcal H}(P-2i). \tag{11}
\]
Moreover, negation shows that \(|\mathcal U|=2|\mathcal H|\), and
\[
|\mathcal U|=\varphi=p^{r-1}(p-1).
\]
Thus (10) and (11) give
\[
L=2^{2|\mathcal H|}=2^\varphi. \tag{12}
\]

Now consider
\[
T:=\prod_{i\in\mathcal H}(1-Pu_i).
\]
Its second-order expansion is
\[
T=1-PH_1+P^2c(H_1^2-H_2). \tag{13}
\]
On the other hand, squaring the right side of (9), discarding terms containing \(P^3\), and using (6), which says \(P^2H_2=0\) in \(R\), gives exactly the right side of (13). Hence
\[
T=L^2=4^\varphi. \tag{14}
\]
Finally,
\[
B_-=
\prod_{i\in\mathcal H}i(1-P/i)=B_0T,
\]
so (8) follows.

We now derive a shift law for all half blocks. First observe that
\[
B_1B_-=B_0^2. \tag{15}
\]
Indeed,
\[
(i+P)(i-P)=i^2\left(1-P^2i^{-2}\right).
\]
When these factors are multiplied, all products of two correction terms vanish because they contain \(P^4\), and the sum of the correction terms vanishes by (6). Thus their product is \(1\), proving (15). Combining (8) and (15), and cancelling the unit \(B_0\), gives
\[
4^\varphi B_1=B_0. \tag{16}
\]

There is also a cross-multiplication identity
\[
B_{q+1}B_0=B_qB_1\qquad(q\geq0). \tag{17}
\]
For completeness, compare the individual products
\[
(i+(q+1)P)i
\quad\text{and}\quad
(i+qP)(i+P).
\]
Their difference is \(-qP^2\). Thus
\[
(i+(q+1)P)i=(i+qP)(i+P)
 \left(1-qP^2((i+qP)(i+P))^{-1}\right).
\]
Modulo \(P\), the inverse in the correction term reduces to \(i^{-2}\). Therefore the sum of the correction terms vanishes modulo \(P^3\) by (6), while every product of two correction terms contains \(P^4\) and also vanishes. The product of all correction factors is consequently \(1\), which proves (17).

Using (16) in (17) and cancelling the unit \(B_1\), we obtain the one-step shift law
\[
4^\varphi B_{q+1}=B_q. \tag{18}
\]
Iteration gives, for every \(N,q\geq0\),
\[
4^{N\varphi}B_{q+N}=B_q\quad\text{in }R. \tag{19}
\]
The case \(N=3n\) will be used in the odd-index argument.

## 3. Exact factorial block decompositions

The following identities are equalities of positive integers, not merely congruences.

For every \(N\geq0\),
\[
(NP)!=p^{Np^{r-1}}(Np^{r-1})!
 \prod_{q=0}^{N-1}\prod_{i\in\mathcal U}(qP+i). \tag{20}
\]
To prove this, separate the factors in \((NP)!\) divisible by \(p\) from those not divisible by \(p\). The divisible factors contribute
\[
p^{Np^{r-1}}(Np^{r-1})!,
\]
and the remaining factors form \(N\) consecutive complete reduced-residue blocks of length \(P\), giving the displayed product.

In the notation above, (20) implies, for all \(C,m\geq0\),
\[
(Cmp^r)!=p^{Cmp^{r-1}}(Cmp^{r-1})!\,U(C,m). \tag{21}
\]

We also need a half-factorial version. Suppose \(C n\) is odd, and put
\[
M=\frac{Cn-1}{2}.
\]
Define the natural-number shifted half block
\[
H_M:=\prod_{i\in\mathcal H}(MP+i). \tag{22}
\]
Then
\[
\left(\frac{Cnp^r-1}{2}\right)!
 =p^{(Cnp^{r-1}-1)/2}
  \left(\frac{Cnp^{r-1}-1}{2}\right)!
  U(1,M)H_M. \tag{23}
\]
Here is the block decomposition behind (23). Since both \(Cn\) and \(P\) are odd,
\[
\frac{CnP-1}{2}=MP+\frac{P-1}{2}.
\]
Split the factorial at \(MP\). Applying (20) to \((MP)!\) supplies the complete blocks \(U(1,M)\). In the remaining interval of length \((P-1)/2\), the multiples of \(p\) are
\[
MP+p,\ MP+2p,\ldots,
\]
and, after division by \(p\), they give exactly the tail needed to extend \((Mp^{r-1})!\) to
\[
\left(\frac{Cnp^{r-1}-1}{2}\right)!.
\]
The factors not divisible by \(p\) in this last half interval are precisely \(MP+i\) with \(i\in\mathcal H\), producing \(H_M\). Counting the removed multiples of \(p\), together with the exponent from (20), gives the exponent \((Cnp^{r-1}-1)/2\). This proves (23).

Upon reduction modulo \(P^3\), the product \(H_M\) is exactly the half block \(B_M\) from (7).

## 4. Even base index

Suppose first that \(n=2k\). Since all Gamma arguments are then integers,
\[
a(2k)=\frac{(18k)!(4k)!(3k)!}{(9k)!(8k)!(6k)!(2k)!}. \tag{24}
\]
Set
\[
N(k)=(18k)!(4k)!(3k)!,
\qquad
D(k)=(9k)!(8k)!(6k)!(2k)!.
\]
The integrality hypothesis and (24) imply the exact integer identity
\[
A_{2k}D(k)=N(k). \tag{25}
\]

Applying (21) to the three numerator factorials gives
\[
N(kp^r)=p^{25kp^{r-1}}N(kp^{r-1})\,U_N,
\]
where
\[
U_N=U(18,k)U(4,k)U(3,k).
\]
Likewise,
\[
D(kp^r)=p^{25kp^{r-1}}D(kp^{r-1})\,U_D,
\]
where
\[
U_D=U(9,k)U(8,k)U(6,k)U(2,k).
\]
The exponent \(25kp^{r-1}\) is the same on both sides because
\[
18+4+3=9+8+6+2=25.
\]
Use (25) at levels \(r\) and \(r-1\), substitute these decompositions, and cancel the common positive integer
\(p^{25kp^{r-1}}D(kp^{r-1})\). We obtain
\[
A_{2kp^r}U_D=A_{2kp^{r-1}}U_N. \tag{26}
\]

By the complete-block congruence (5),
\[
U_N\equiv W^{(18+4+3)k}=W^{25k}\pmod {P^3},
\]
\[
U_D\equiv W^{(9+8+6+2)k}=W^{25k}\pmod {P^3}.
\]
Thus \(U_N\equiv U_D\pmod {P^3}\). Moreover, \(U_D\) is a unit modulo \(P^3\). Reducing (26) modulo \(P^3\) and cancelling this unit yields
\[
A_{2kp^r}\equiv A_{2kp^{r-1}}\pmod {P^3}. \tag{27}
\]
This proves the desired congruence when \(n\) is even.

## 5. Odd base index

Now suppose that \(n\) is odd. We first rewrite the Gamma quotient entirely in factorial form. The standard half-integer Gamma identity is
\[
\Gamma\left(j+\frac12\right)
 =\frac{(2j-1)!!}{2^j}\sqrt\pi.
\]
Using this for the two half-integral Gamma factors, and then using
\[
(2j)!=2^j j!(2j-1)!!,
\]
one obtains, for every odd \(m\),
\[
a(m)=\frac{4^{3m}\left(\frac{9m-1}{2}\right)!(2m)!}
 {\left(\frac{3m-1}{2}\right)!(4m)!m!}. \tag{28}
\]
For example, writing \(m=2k+1\), the numerator becomes
\(4^{6k+3}(9k+4)!(4k+2)!\), and the denominator becomes
\((3k+1)!(8k+4)!(2k+1)!\), which is exactly (28).

Define
\[
N_o(m)=4^{3m}\left(\frac{9m-1}{2}\right)!(2m)!,
\]
\[
D_o(m)=\left(\frac{3m-1}{2}\right)!(4m)!m!.
\]
Then, for odd \(m\), integrality and (28) give
\[
A_mD_o(m)=N_o(m). \tag{29}
\]
Since \(p\) is odd, both \(np^r\) and \(np^{r-1}\) are odd.

Put
\[
x=np^{r-1},\qquad
q_9=\frac{9n-1}{2},\qquad q_3=\frac{3n-1}{2}.
\]
Because \(n\) is odd,
\[
q_9=q_3+3n. \tag{30}
\]
Also
\[
\frac{9x-1}{2}+2x
 =\frac{3x-1}{2}+4x+x. \tag{31}
\]
This identity will balance all powers of \(p\).

Apply the half-factorial decomposition (23) with \(C=9\), and the full decomposition (21) with \(C=2\). Also use
\[
3np^r=3np^{r-1}+3n\,p^{r-1}(p-1),
\]
which splits the power of \(4\). We get
\[
N_o(np^r)=p^E N_o(x)\,V_N, \tag{32}
\]
where
\[
E=\frac{9x-1}{2}+2x
\]
and
\[
V_N=
4^{3n\varphi}\,U(1,q_9)\,U(2,n)\,H_{q_9}. \tag{33}
\]
Likewise, applying (23) with \(C=3\), and (21) with \(C=4\) and \(C=1\), gives
\[
D_o(np^r)=p^E D_o(x)\,V_D, \tag{34}
\]
where equality of the exponent with the same \(E\) follows from (31), and
\[
V_D=U(1,q_3)\,U(4,n)\,U(1,n)\,H_{q_3}. \tag{35}
\]

Use (29) at \(np^r\) and at \(x=np^{r-1}\), substitute (32) and (34), and cancel the common nonzero integer \(p^E D_o(x)\). This gives the exact relation
\[
A_{np^r}V_D=A_{np^{r-1}}V_N. \tag{36}
\]

It remains to compare the two \(p\)-free multipliers modulo \(P^3\). By (5),
\[
U(1,q_9)U(2,n)\equiv W^{q_9+2n},

after reduction modulo \(P^3\), while
\[
U(1,q_3)U(4,n)U(1,n)\equiv W^{q_3+5n}.
\]
By (30),
\[
q_9+2n=q_3+5n, \tag{37}
\]
so the complete-block powers of \(W\) agree.

The remaining factors agree by the half-block shift formula (19). Since \(H_q\) reduces to \(B_q\), equations (19) and (30), with \(N=3n\), give
\[
4^{3n\varphi}H_{q_9}
 \equiv H_{q_3}\pmod {P^3}. \tag{38}
\]
Combining (33), (35), (37), and (38), we obtain
\[
V_N\equiv V_D\pmod {P^3}. \tag{39}
\]
Every factor in \(V_D\) is prime to \(p\): this is clear for the complete blocks, and each factor of \(H_{q_3}\) is \(q_3P+i\) with \(p\nmid i\). Hence \(V_D\) is a unit modulo \(P^3\).

Reduce (36) modulo \(P^3\), replace \(V_N\) by \(V_D\) using (39), and cancel the unit \(V_D\). We conclude that
\[
A_{np^r}\equiv A_{np^{r-1}}\pmod {P^3} \tag{40}
\]
when \(n\) is odd.

Every positive integer \(n\) is either even or odd. Equation (27) handles the even case and (40) handles the odd case. Since \(P^3=(p^r)^3=p^{3r}\), in all cases
\[
A_{np^r}\equiv A_{np^{r-1}}\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\]
As \(A_m\) is the integer represented by \(a(m)\), this is precisely
\[
\boxed{a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r}}},
\]
for every prime \(p\geq5\) and all positive integers \(n,r\), under the stated integrality assumption.
